titlePlain: How to Honestly Benchmark a Quantum
subtitle: Lesson 31 · Algorithm Benchmarking Against Classical Alternatives

eyebrow: A habit this course has used all along

steps.label: 1. Compare against the BEST known classical algorithm
steps.sub: Beating trial division isn't a benchmark of Shor's — beating GNFS is

steps.label: 2. Be precise about what's being counted
steps.sub: Query complexity, gate complexity, and wall-clock time are three different numbers

steps.label: "O(√N) steps" only holds if "step" means one oracle query
steps.sub: Each query is itself a circuit — building it is not free

steps.label: State which metric you mean, every time
steps.sub: Conflating them is the single most common error in popular coverage

eyebrow: Rule 3: the hardware gap is real
code:
Shor's algorithm: polynomial-time, mathematically sound
Gidney & Ekera (2019): ~20,000,000 noisy qubits, ~8 hours
  -> to factor one RSA-2048 modulus

"Asymptotically superior" != "deployable this year"
caption: An honest benchmark separates these two claims explicitly and states which one it's making.

eyebrow: Rules 4 & 5, applied to this course itself

steps.label: 4. Asymptotic superiority ≠ superiority at real sizes
steps.sub: A classical linear scan can simply be faster today, even if it's "worse" at scale

steps.label: 5. State the promise and the error model explicitly
steps.sub: Deutsch-Jozsa and Simon's assume guarantees real data never has

steps.label: Chapters 1–6 already did this, lesson by lesson
steps.sub: BQP ≠ NP, Grover's overshoot table, RSA's hardware gap, HHL's caveats

steps.label: This checklist just names what the course has been doing
steps.sub: Apply it to any quantum-advantage claim you hear next
